book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
samples: In this memoir (book Chapter 1, 'A Cannabis Odyssey'), Harvard psychiatrist Lester Grinspoon recounts how his 1967 review of the anti-marijuana literature convinced him he had been 'brainwashed' by a fear-based 'cannabis catechism,' coining 'cannabinophobia' and likening it to the 'madness of crowds.' He argues from personal use — hearing Sgt. Pepper for the first time, quitting psychoanalysis after 'stoned' self-critiques — that beyond recreation and medicine there is a third category, 'enhancement.' The piece is autobiographical drug-policy advocacy rather than the application of a specific named philosopher.

Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.

Hathaway and Sharpley analyze the cannabis experience of medical-'compassion club' users through Csikszentmihalyi's concept of 'flow.' They ground flow in William James's 'stream of consciousness' and in Taoism, reading Tao as 'a patterned flow of the universe' and wu wei as the effortless equilibrium users describe ('it just centers me,' 'I take an inventory on my soul'). Against Western monophasic medicine, they defend users' 'anecdotal' testimony as legitimate knowledge of a body–mind–spirit balance that cannabis restores.

Montagne's 'Buzz, High, and Stoned' argues that the cannabis experience is largely constituted by the metaphors users apply to it. Tracing hashish descriptions from Gautier, Baudelaire, Bayard Taylor, Ludlow and jazzman Mezz Mezzrow to modern song lyrics and Robert Crumb's 'Stoned Agin!' cartoon, he maps 'buzz,' 'high' and 'stoned' onto dose-dependent levels documented by Moreau (1845) and Charles Tart, and shows the words carry more meaning than pharmacology, shaping set, setting and behavior. The Greek 'pharmakon' (remedy/poison/charm) frames the analysis of meaning-making in drug language.

Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.

Clack's 'Cannabis and the Human Condition' reads intoxication through Freud's Civilization and its Discontents, where drugs are the 'crudest but most effective' palliative against a life 'too hard for us,' tied to the pleasure principle and the Nirvana/death-instinct drive to discharge stimulus. He supplements Freud with Schopenhauer's pessimism — life oscillating between suffering and boredom — to add 'stimulus hunger' Freud ignored, arguing cannabis both dampens and stokes the 'fire in the brain' depending on THC potency (high vs. stoned). He concludes that, like religion, art and love, cannabis augments a bleak existence, so 'all cannabis use is medicinal.'

book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
samples: Hans Florine's foreword frames climbing as a way of posing philosophical questions rather than settling them, echoing the book's 'it's the journey' ethos, and previews debates the volume takes up: the sanity/morality of free soloing, hold chipping, and how routes are graded. Florine describes himself as an Ayn Rand Objectivist who also carries Buddhist concern and treats logic as a reliable tool, and calls the 100-percent focus of climbing 'physical meditation.' No taxonomy philosopher (Rand) is actually deployed in argument; the piece is a personal, agenda-setting foreword rather than a sustained application of a philosophical position.

Schmid's editorial introduction reads climbing through Tejada-Flores' 'Games Climbers Play,' arguing that each climbing game (bouldering, trad, expedition) has its own rules and that climbing ethically means respecting the rules of the game one plays, with 'better style' meaning voluntarily adopting more restrictive rules. Invoking Russell on the value of philosophy and Mallory's 'because it's there,' he surveys the volume's essays and their applied-ethical questions about risk, free soloing, hold manufacturing, and environmental impact. The piece is a map of the book's terrain rather than an argument for one doctrine, previewing Krein's Stoic freedom, Treanor's Aristotelian virtue, Levey's Hegel, and Swan's Zen.

Kevin Krein argues that the freedom climbers report feeling is not freedom of movement, political freedom, or free will—on those measures a roped climber pinned on a ledge is less free—but the Stoic freedom of aligning one's will with what nature allows. Using Chrysippus' tethered-dog image and the Stoic identification of human logos with cosmic reason, he claims the climber who understands and accepts the mountain's conditions and wills only what it permits becomes free, which is why experienced climbers feel freest when their options are fewest. He adds Epictetus' dichotomy of control: the mountain (storms, avalanches, one's own failing body) is largely outside our power, so limiting desire to what we control—composure, choices, effort—is how a climber stays free in any conditions.

Prompted by the avalanche death of his climbing partner Charlie on the Super Couloir, Paul Charlton uses Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism to ask whether the risks of climbing can be ethically justified, insisting that blindly accepting risk is indefensible but deliberate, reasoned risk can be right. He weighs climbing's costs (frivolity, self-focus, danger to self and to grieving family) against its intrinsic value (joy, friendship, aesthetic experience) and instrumental value (cultivating human excellence, psychological growth, reprioritized lives), invoking Mill's higher/lower pleasures to argue quality of happiness matters, not just quantity. His conclusion is that climbing can be justified only when it produces more overall good than any alternative use of that time, leaving each climber to run the calculation for their own case.

Joe Fitschen distinguishes justifying climbing (weak, self-revealing answers) from explaining why humans climb, and offers an evolutionary, naturalistic explanation: the ability and pleasure of climbing are inherited arboreal dispositions that were not selected out and can still have utility, so Mallory's 'because it's there' names a real, gene-rooted urge. He deploys Wittgenstein's analysis of 'game' and family resemblances to block the fallacy of universality—the fact that some people lack the urge to climb says nothing against its evolutionary roots—and warns against teleological thinking about traits. He also treats climbing's pleasures (physical, aesthetic, emotional) and its style-based ethics (bolting disputes, ego vs. the pleasure of the experience) as expressions of an evolved, social human nature.

Heidi Howkins Lockwood examines the 'asymmetry thesis'—that a climber's gratuitous risk is less acceptable than an astronaut's necessary risk—and argues its two standard defenses fail: the Rule of Rescue is neither necessary (free soloists need no rescue yet are condemned) nor sufficient (Hornbein and Unsoeld's risky Everest traverse was praised because it succeeded), and the argument from compassion collapses into circularity. She then shows the intuition is really driven by external background assumptions, especially gender inequality: the media vilified climber-mother Alison Hargreaves while lauding astronaut-mother Christa McAuliffe, because ambition-for-profit violates the 'traditionally female' role of service. She concedes a limited, defensible version tied to the assumption that seeking risk as a mere end (rather than an ineliminable means) is irresponsible.

samples: This foreword by Rocky Rakovic, editor of Inked magazine, argues that tattoos were a 'harbinger of Twitter' – both are technologies of everyman self-expression born of a 'me generation' told it could be anything. It traces how reality-TV shows like Miami Ink and LA Ink, and figures such as Kat Von D, moved tattooing from the sailor-and-scofflaw margins into mainstream fashion, citing the Pew figure that forty percent of Americans aged 26–40 are tattooed. The connection to philosophy is thematic rather than argued: ink as individualist fashion that lets people 'scream their identity on their skin.'

Robert Arp's introduction takes Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' and its mind–body dualism (the conceivability argument that mind is distinct from body) and inverts it into the book's motto 'I am, therefore I ink': the tattooed person insists identity is bodily-based self-expression, challenging the Cartesian idea that the essential self is a non-bodily thinking thing. Arp flags Descartes' possible question-begging, then previews each chapter, framing tattoos as fertile ground for the philosophy of the person, personal identity over time, and self-expression.

Charles Taliaferro and Mark Odden survey the history and nature of tattooing – from the 3200 BCE Iceman's fifty-seven tattoos and Aetius' Constantinople recipe, through Leviticus' prohibition, Polynesian and Japanese irezumi, to Nazi concentration-camp numbering – to argue tattoos carry competing cultural (public) and individual (private) meanings. They advance a 'double skin' theory: a tattoo is both visible image and buried marking, juxtaposing interiority and exteriority. Their closing Lincoln puzzle ('calling a tail a leg doesn't make it a leg') stresses the body's stubborn reality and the 'inescapable seriousness' of permanently relabeling one's skin.

Juniper Ellis shows tattoos resist any single interpretive scheme by running through cases: Loos and Lacassagne's criminological 'I tattoo, therefore I will commit murder'; the biblical Mark of Cain and St. Paul's stigmata as signs of protection and salvation; Lacan's claim that the tattoo is the first signifier that marks off the human subject; and Pacific tatau (Te Pehi Kupe's moko-as-signature, Queequeg's unreadable Moby-Dick tattoo) that incorporates a person into a collective. She reads Kant's Critique of Judgment dismissal of Maori tattooing and invokes Levinas' 'the face speaks' to argue a tattooed face is eloquent speech, crossing lines between individual and collective, saint and criminal.

Nicolas Michaud asks whether tattoos are art by testing three theories against them: art world (institutional) theory, under which tattoos are not yet art because the artworld has not admitted them; formalism (Clive Bell's 'significant form'), under which a well-composed tattoo qualifies but its human canvas is irrelevant; and Tolstoyan expressionism, under which an emotionally infectious tattoo (his example of a broken-chain tattoo over an abuse survivor's bruise) counts. He concludes tattoos are best understood as performance art – like Duchamp mustaching the Mona Lisa, the living, mortal, changing human canvas adds context and meaning, making tattoos reflect on art and our own death.

Kimberly Baltzer-Jaray and Tanya Rodriguez argue, against George Carlin's 'mobile art gallery' joke, that the only thing separating tattooing from fine art is its fleshy canvas. They show how formalist, expressionist and institutional theories historically excluded both women's craft and tattoos, then use feminist aesthetics (Korsmeyer, Iris Marion Young on the gaze) to reclaim the female tattooed body as an assertion of agency against objectification. They then apply Gadamer's hermeneutics – art as play, festival and symbol – to argue tattoos make a claim on the viewer, build a 'hermeneutic collective' community, and function as inexhaustible symbols prompting self-recognition.

samples: This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.

This span closes the walk-of-shame semiotics and then applies ancient ethics to college relationships. Puka defends long-distance college relationships through Aristotle's account of philia—arguing (provocatively, per Aristotle) that love is an activity, so being apart 'murders' love unless couples make Skype, sexting, and texting into the relationship's real medium rather than a substitute. Stephens brings Epicurus and Lucretius to 'friends with benefits': since sexual passion is a natural-but-unnecessary desire that breeds anxiety and love is a wound to the mind, while friendship is necessary for ataraxia, he concludes students should skip the sex and keep the friend—'friends are the real benefits,' echoing Tina Turner's 'What's Love Got to Do with It?' Levine/Mongeau and Smith/Morrison supply communication-research data on how FWB relationships form, are negotiated (usually not), and often end when one partner 'catches feelings.'

This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.

The essay argues that soaring tuition drives college students into sexual self-commodification—egg-selling ('Pay your tuition with eggs'), craigslist/backpage escorting, and dorm-porn webcam sites like VoyeurDorm and CocoDorm—and reads these cases through Kant's second formulation, condemning them as treating oneself and others as mere means rather than ends of intrinsic dignity. It applies Marx's notion of false consciousness to Natalie Dylan's virginity auction and Ashley Dupré's 'empowerment' claims, comparing them to women choosing high heels as internalized oppression. It uses Rousseau's Social Contract and Mill's On Liberty to argue that prostitution is a form of illegitimate 'voluntary slavery' because one cannot rightly alienate one's own inalienable freedom, and contrasts coerced cases (Helena in Singapore, Rosie Reid's traumatic auctioned deflowering, John Gechter's porn suspension from a Christian college) with less-coerced ones to argue moral concern should track the degree of circumstantial coercion.

book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
samples: Winters reads the Zodiac Killer's taunting letters through Sartre's account of 'the look' from Being and Nothingness. He argues Zodiac's letters function like a snapped twig or a lit window: they make Northern Californians experience themselves as seen objects, hunted 'slaves' and pawns in Zodiac's game rather than free subjects. A phenomenological (first-person) analysis of the fear Zodiac induces, and of how his letters restrict the choices available within our facticity, is offered as superior to psychological or analytic accounts for explaining our fascination with the macabre.

Schmid examines Moors Murderer Ian Brady's book The Gates of Janus, arguing that Brady built a genuine philosophy of serial murder from Sade and Nietzsche rather than merely name-dropping them. He corrects popular caricatures of the ubermensch and will to power, then shows Brady grounds his self-account in moral relativism and reframes serial killing as fundamentally about 'power and the will to power.' Brady's admiration for Carl Panzram and his likeness to the self-justifying, punishment-transcending Sadean hero illustrate how Nietzschean and Sadean ideas actually shape a killer's self-understanding.

Alfano uses the trial of 'Sunset Strip Killer' Doug Clark to argue that situational forces and attribution biases may have swayed his jury regardless of the actual evidence. Drawing on Milgram's obedience study, Zimbardo's prison simulation, Knobe's intentionality vignettes, and Haidt's disgust experiments, he shows how gender bias, pretrial media, and revulsion at Clark's necrophilia could distort judgments of guilt. He closes with Nozick's truth-tracking account of knowledge to press whether a juror who would have convicted anyway can be said to know Clark is guilty.

Howard surveys serial killers from Liu Pengli and Locusta through Gilles de Rais, Bathory, Bichel, Panzram, and modern killers she interviewed (Bobby Joe Long, Shawcross, Milat, Birnie) to illustrate 'practical moral skepticism': the thesis that one can know right from wrong yet feel no motivation to be good. She distinguishes this from epistemic moral skepticism and argues that many killers, often privileged or unconstrained, understood moral codes but were driven instead by power, sadism, fatigue, or anger, showing that a failure of moral motivation is ancient rather than modern.

Vargas argues that a psychopathic serial killer can be profoundly evil yet not morally responsible. Reviewing the clinical literature (Hare, the moral/conventional rule distinction, the 'mrah'/harm thought experiment), he holds that psychopaths are blind to moral rules and so, since blame requires understanding wrongdoing, cannot be blamed — the appropriate response is quarantine rather than resentment. He then separates evil from responsibility: to be evil is to desire others' harm for its own sake, and such evil, like being a jerk, need not be something one is responsible for, which is why psychopathic killers can be genuinely evil though not blameworthy.

Brophy puts Showtime's Dexter Morgan on 'ethical trial' before the reader-as-jury, applying four tests. Utilitarianism approves because killing killers maximizes happiness (the Ticking Time Bomb analogy); Kant's categorical imperative and even Kant's own endorsement of executing murderers cast Dexter as a 'just executioner' applying a dark golden rule; virtue theory finds Dexter progressing toward moderation and flourishing as a 'warrior' in his social role; and Rawls's veil of ignorance suggests one would consent to Dexter patrolling one's neighborhood. Brophy concludes Dexter is morally excusable, perhaps praiseworthy.

book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
samples: John Friend's foreword surveys yoga's three classical philosophical systems and connects them to how modern Hatha yoga is practiced: Classical (Patanjali) yoga as separating purusha (spirit) from prakriti (matter) to reach kaivalya; Vedanta as neutralizing maya to realize the unity of atman with the supreme; and non-dual Tantra, from which Hatha yoga derives, treating body and mind as frequencies of one divine Shiva-Shakti energy. It argues yoga's enduring claim is that the essential self is free, and that direct lived experience of that freedom outranks merely intellectual knowledge of the texts.

Editor Liz Stillwaggon Swan uses her rejection of Descartes' mind–body dualism to reinterpret yoga's promise of 'union.' Drawing on Spinoza's view that mind and matter are two aspects of a single reality, she argues 'mind' is just a placeholder for embodied abilities, so a yogi who denies a separate spirit cannot literally 'unite' mind and body — they are already one. She reframes yogic union (via Megan Burke's essay) as uniting self with nature, and defends practicing yoga for physical and psychological benefit without any spiritual claim, likening secularized yoga to secular Christmas.

Jennifer Munyer's 'How Yoga Won the West' narrates yoga's evolution — from the Pashupati seal and the Pre-Vedic age through the Vedas, Upanishads, Patanjali's Yoga Sutras and Raja yoga, to Krishnamacharya's traveling 'circuses,' Vivekananda, and Indra Devi. Her governing argument is that yoga's outer form constantly changes to fit each culture while its essence (union with the divine) stays the same, a claim she illustrates with the idea that a person changes appearance over a lifetime yet remains the same self — a lay expression of impermanence of form beneath continuity.

Kieran McManus's travel memoir 'Will I Find My Guru in India?' recounts his search from Kathmandu to Rishikesh and the Agama Yoga School, where teacher Kushru's lectures on karma, breath, and diet finally make asana click for him. His reported insight — that every thought and act moves him toward or away from his sacred potential, and that the yogi transcends suffering by treating each experience as neutral and as an opportunity, remaining present — applies a karmic and present-moment ethic to his own practice rather than expounding doctrine abstractly.

David Robles's 'The Seeker' argues that declining trust in Western absolutist religion drives people toward yoga as an experiential, self-directed spirituality. His central move is that Patanjali's Yoga Sutras rank direct perception above testimony and scripture — mirroring the scientific method — so yoga functions as a 'spiritual science' harmonious with empiricism, whereas established religion rests on second-hand revelation. He distinguishes 'spiritual' (personal, inspiration-based) from 'religious' (culturally binding dogma) and casts the American 'seeker' as building a better, results-oriented, pragmatic spirituality.

Purcell and Shaffer's 'Men, Sports, and Yoga' asks why, though yoga began as a male discipline, ~80% of US practitioners are women, using the stories of three men (Mark, Carl, Jake) taught privately to avoid the competitive self-consciousness of group classes. Its philosophical thread is the ego (ahamkara, 'the I-maker'): rather than obliterating the ego, the men learn to keep it in check and channel competitiveness inward against their own limits, so 'unifying mind and body' turns out to be a competitive sport that works by managing one's own drives and self-image.

book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
samples: In this foreword, Alligator Records founder Bruce Iglauer argues that the blues is 'magic' rooted in the specific 300-year African-American experience of slavery, sharecropping, and Jim Crow, yet reaches a worldwide audience. He dissects the 'tension and release' at the music's core — delayed vocals, notes bent up to pitch, Muddy Waters' slide, Albert King's guitar — as the mechanism of its emotional effect, and contrasts the communal call-and-response of black juke joints with the more passive reception of white festival audiences. The piece is a practitioner's testimony rather than a sustained philosophical argument, so no taxonomy philosopher's doctrine is genuinely applied.

The editors' introduction argues blues and philosophy are close kin in confronting the struggling soul. It reads Lightnin' Hopkins's 'Lonesome Dog' through Plato's tripartite soul from Republic IX — the howling 'dog' is the appetitive part — but claims the blues achieves a 'blues harmony' rather than Plato's reason-ruled harmony. It casts Socrates, calm before execution in the Phaedo, as having a 'bluesy sensibility' that rises above worry through philosophizing, invokes Bentham's claim that the capacity to suffer is what matters morally to gloss the blues as knowledge of suffering, and likens the blues' triumphant affirmation to Nietzsche's positivity.

Joel Rudinow stages a three-way internal dialogue ('Me,' 'Myself,' and 'I') debating whether the commercialized, white-inflected blues — the House of Blues chain, the Blues Brothers, Cyndi Lauper's Memphis Blues, Clapton's Cream 'Crossroads' — is still really the blues. 'I' introduces Heraclitus's doctrine that everything flows and you cannot step twice into the same river, using the Heraclitean flux of culture to argue the blues is a living, ever-changing tradition whose 'canon' cannot be pinned to a fixed time, place, or racial purity, dissolving the survive/thrive/arrive question into one about how a canon forms and evolves.

Ken Ueno recounts a B. B. King lecture where King played the 'right' notes, then 'turned it on' with identical notes made electric by personality, to argue that the blues locates a song's identity in the performer's aura rather than a written score. He appropriates Walter Benjamin's 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' but inverts it: where Benjamin held that mechanical reproduction withers the aura, Ueno claims recordings actually preserve and transmit the aura of blues performers (bent notes, B. B.'s voice) that classical notation cannot capture, making recordings a more democratic notation for an aural tradition.

Wade Fox and Richard Greene argue that no set of necessary and sufficient conditions — twelve-bar structure, AAB lyrics, mournful content — defines the blues, since paradigm cases violate each (Charley Patton's one-chord songs, cheerful jug band tunes, instrumentals). Invoking the 'Socratic fallacy,' they deny that failure to define a term means failure to grasp it, then apply Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations notion of family resemblance so that blues songs share overlapping features without a common essence. They extend this to argue contemporary blues (Stevie Ray Vaughan, Robert Cray, Jonny Lang) are 'twelve-bar zombies' — resembling the blues but lacking the lived authenticity that gives it a soul.

Philip Jenkins distinguishes the blues as musical form from the blues as cultural expression, defending a version of Amiri Baraka's expressivist claim that white musicians (imagining Barry Manilow) cannot authentically play the blues. Against the formalism of Rudinow and James O. Young, he theorizes that one's expressive 'options' are internalized from one's social group, so authentic blues requires the lived, embodied experience of African-American oppression that a cultural outsider lacks. He roots the disagreement in a 'too-loose' definition of culture that ignores how involuntary, systematic oppression makes African-American culture more experientially cohesive than voluntary subcultures.

book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
samples: In this foreword Joshua Wolf Shenk recounts an intoxicating blind date with 'Rachael' to argue that dating exposes the core existential dilemma of social creatures: we crave ecstasy (ekstasis, 'standing outside oneself') yet can only connect by holding on to a discrete identity. He blames the modern isolation of the self on Descartes' claim that the self inhabits its own subjective realm and Hobbes' picture of natural man as solitary, and cites Camus that once you choose to live, the real question is how to relate to others. His unresolved paradox—needing the mantra 'I was complete before I met you' while knowing it is false—frames love as the tension between self-sufficiency and merger.

Editors Kristie Miller and Marlene Clark introduce the volume by opening with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics claim that the human drive to couple is even stronger than the drive to live as a political being and that fulfillment rests in loving relationships. They frame dating as a rule-governed 'game' with aims and strategies and preview each contributor's essay—Jenkins on flirting, Langan on conservative men, Samp and Cohen against unconditional love, the elevator metaphor, cyberdating, evolutionary seduction, and Colyvan's game-theoretic mate search—tying age-old ethical questions about treating partners well to new work in evolutionary psychology, decision theory, and the ethics of online romance.

Carrie Jenkins does analytic conceptual analysis of flirting, rejecting the Oxford English Dictionary's claim that flirting requires having no serious intentions. She distinguishes 'flirting' from merely 'behaving flirtatiously' (Joe who over-holds eye contact, the tourist touching her earlobe in Italy are flirtatious without flirting) and argues flirting requires an intention to act in ways disposed to raise flirter-flirtee romance to salience, done in a 'knowing yet playful' way. Borrowing Kripke's 'killer yellow' to imagine 'killer-flirts' who die on contact, and citing chatbot studies, she concludes one can flirt with an imagined or non-human target only if one believes it can respond significantly.

Emily Langan uses focus-group data from 75 self-described ideologically conservative, mostly Christian young men to argue that flirting is a site of moral decision-making, opening with Hitch's 'right broom' line to show these men reject its libido-driven premise. She reports three shared themes—flirting is not about sex but about honesty of motive, timing within a relationship's stages, and reciprocity ('it has to be a two-way street')—and three tensions (healthy vs. harmful, superficial vs. serious, overt vs. covert), drawing on courtship-stage and flirting-style research to show that, contrary to the stereotype that only women agonize over relationships, conservative men wrestle with being 'risqué yet respectable.'

Jennifer Samp and Andrew Cohen argue against the Notebook-style romantic ideal of unconditional love, casting dating as a 'calculated exchange' explained by social-exchange and interdependence theory (comparison level and comparison level of alternatives). Adopting Aristotle's distinction between friendships of utility/pleasure and 'complete friendships' in which one values the friend as 'another self' and as an end in itself, they hold the best romances are complete friendships—yet insist even these must be conditioned. Their key thought experiment: a genuinely boundless love would survive discovering one's partner is a child-molesting murderer; since it should not, 'true love knows bounds' and remains part of a good life only because it can be defeated by such reasons.

John Rowan and Patricia Hallen build an extended elevator metaphor for dating (Ann and Bob riding floors, pushing buttons to raise or lower intimacy, gravity pulling toward breakup) to capture Heraclitus's insight that a relationship is a reality in constant change, while invoking Plato to insist the conceptual reality of a relationship is as real as physical objects. They define dating as gauging the possibility of eventual commitment, cite Hume's canoe image for implicit communication of shared destination, and ground their strategies—be yourself, go slowly, communicate, befriend—in Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating honesty, courage, and loyalty as habits lying in the golden mean between deficiency and excess (e.g., the Look Who's Talking date who overshares is 'excessively honest').

Shock Value A Deleuzean Encounter with James Purdy's Narrow Rooms

samples: Thomas Fahy's editorial introduction frames the volume by comparing horror to his skydiving experience: both offer the thrill of confronting danger within a promise of safety. He organizes the collection's essays around morality, identity, cultural history, and aesthetics, previewing how each contributor yokes a pop-culture horror text to a philosopher (Nickel's skeptical reading of Psycho/The Birds, Morris on Kant and torture-horror, his own Hobbes reading of In Cold Blood, Lutz's Marx and Land of the Dead). He argues horror's 'play,' hybridity, and repetition let it raise questions about fear, suffering, justice, and the human capacity for violence.

Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.

Philip Tallon extends Aristotle's Poetics from tragedy to horror, arguing that where tragedy elicits pity and fear, horror mirrors the characters' visceral revulsion in the audience. Frankenstein serves as an internal critique of Enlightenment hubris, Victor's overreach making the abandoned monster more sympathetic than his creator. Against Lyotard's postmodern 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' and moral relativism, Tallon claims horror (e.g., King's 'Salem's Lot, where a priest craves a real EVIL to fight) works by violating an intuited moral, natural, and social order, thereby revealing a commonly-denied but underlying objective sense of morality and evil.

Jeremy Morris analyzes torture-horror through two questions: is the torture justified, and is the audience's enjoyment justified? He reads Saw's Jigsaw traps, Seven, and Last House on the Left as explorations of Kantian retributivism and lex talionis, where punishing the autonomous wrongdoer respects his autonomy. For purely sadistic films like Hostel, The Devil's Rejects, and Texas Chainsaw Massacre, he argues (via Humean sentimentalism against Kantian rationalism) that Cook's or Otis and Baby's infectious glee makes the torturer's delight the source of horror. A fully empathetic viewer can share both the victim's suffering and the torturer's joy without endorsing torture, so the genre is not immoral 'torture-porn.'

Thomas Fahy reads Capote's In Cold Blood as horror (the Clutter killers Hickock and Smith as 'realistic monsters' whose human shape terrifies because anyone could be like them) and maps it onto Hobbes's Leviathan. Hickock and Smith act in a Hobbesian state of nature, driven by appetite, power, and moral relativism without remorse. Herb Clutter functions as a Hobbesian sovereign whose Eden-like farm and community collapse into decay, mistrust, and 'war of all against all' after his murder. Fahy also casts Capote himself as a sovereign who, via Foucault's panopticon, imposes a fictionalized cathartic ending, though the book's Hobbesian message is that we all have the potential to kill.

Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.

book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
samples: Rowlands introduces the 'sci-phi' project: science fiction confronts us with the alien 'other' as a mirror in which we understand ourselves, so lowbrow sci-fi films like The Matrix, Total Recall and Starship Troopers make abstract philosophy concrete. He argues philosophy is doing rather than knowing, invoking Fishburne's 'know the path vs walk the path' line and Nietzsche's dictum that one repays a teacher poorly by remaining a pupil. He mentions his own earlier 'fyborg' thesis that human cognition is embedded in the wider informational environment, prefiguring the extended mind.

Using the De Niro monster of Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Rowlands argues absurdity arises from a clash between the view of ourselves from the inside (a locus of meaning) and from the outside (sub specie aeternitatis, insignificant). The monster is assembled from second-hand parts and thrown into a hostile world he did not choose, just as we are stitched together by genes and environment we did not choose (Sartre/Heidegger thrownness). He develops Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, arguing the horror is futility not difficulty, to frame the problem of the meaning of life that underlies every deep philosophical problem.

Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.

Rowlands uses the Terminator cyborg to pose the mind-body problem: how the inside view (consciousness, intentionality) meshes with the outside view (neurons firing). He rejects dualism because it only says what mind is not and cannot explain mind-body interaction (no mass, so no momentum/energy transfer), and because it would make intelligent-machine sci-fi impossible. He argues for materialism, then distinguishes 'nerd' symbol-crunching AI (Schank's restaurant scripts, Deep Blue) from 'jock' neural-network, embodied designs as the route to building an intelligent Terminator that can flexibly respond like Arnie mugging the biker.

Rowlands treats Total Recall as a defence of the memory (psychological-continuity) theory of personal identity: erasing Quaid's memories and restoring Hauser's is an essential change that ends Quaid, so he fights for his existence. He works through and rejects the soul theory (dualism's problems) and body/brain theories via head-transplant and neuron-replacement thought experiments, distinguishing Aristotle's essential/accidental change and Heraclitus's river. The Sixth Day's cloning raises Parfit's fission/duplication problem: a double success cannot be a failure, driving him to abandon identity for a Heraclitean 'river of selves' bound by survival, not identity.

Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.
